newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan mulling liquor tax review after WTO ruling.
newsitem.headline: Japan mulling liquor tax review after WTO ruling.

text.p: Japan said on Friday it would consider revising its liquor taxes as part of a broader fiscal review later this year following a WTO ruling that its duties on spirits break international trade rules.

The World Trade Organisation (WTO), ruling on a complaint by the European Union, the United States and Canada, has found that Japan taxes imported spirits unfairly compared with domestic liquor, Japanese government officials said.

Finance Minister Wataru Kubo told a news conference that the decision by the WTO was severe, but his ministry said it would consider making tax changes in the context of a broader review of taxation to be conducted later this year.
The European Union has said that Japan taxes imported spirits at rates more than six times those imposed on popular domestic products called shochu.

Tokyo has argued that shochu -- a potent, colourless liquor made from barley -- is basically a beverage for poorer people, while whiskey and other imported spirits are drunk by more affluent consumers who can afford to pay more.
A senior Finance Ministry official told reporters that the ministry, at the moment, has no specific ideas as to how to respond to the WTO ruling.
"But I am sure revisions of liquor taxes will be carried out in a revision of overall tax for the next fiscal year," the official said.

Japan carries out a review of its entire taxation system toward the end of every the year and relevant legislation is submitted to parliament early the following year. This would take effect from the start of the fiscal year on April 1.
Following past European calls for a change in Japan's taxes on spirits, Japan gradually revised domestic tax rates, but it failed to satisfy foreign liquor makers.

Further revisions are likely to involve a limited increase in taxes on domestically produced shochu, rather than a cut in taxes on imported whiskey and other spirits as Japan needs the revenue from those because of mounting debts, analysts said.
Industry analysts said Japan's liquor industry was not likely to suffer much from the WTO action as shochu would likely remain the cheapest alcohol in the country.

The WTO panel had been considering Japan's appeal against an initial ruling in July that Tokyo's liquor taxes treat imported spirits such as whiskey and brandy unfairly, to the advantage of domestic products.
Any increase in shochu taxes will be minimal to protect Japanese brewers, analysts said. ($1=111 yen)
